opus-5.5.text:
I think the core realization for us was that a lot of the early work in embodied AI was, frankly, borrowing too much from other domains. We took architectures and training recipes that worked beautifully for language or for internet images, and we tried to bolt them onto robots. And it sort of worked, enough to make nice demos, but every time we pushed toward real deployment, we kept hitting the same walls.

The physical world just has different requirements. Language models live in a world of tokens where you can afford to think for a while, and if you get something slightly wrong, the cost is a bad sentence. A robot is operating in continuous space and continuous time. It has to react within milliseconds, it has to deal with contact, friction, deformable objects, occlusion, and if it makes a mistake, something breaks or someone could get hurt. So latency, precision, and safety aren't secondary metrics you optimize later. They're the foundation.

The other thing is understanding of 3D structure and dynamics. Internet video and images give you a lot of semantic knowledge, what a cup is, what a kitchen looks like, but they don't really teach you how much force it takes to open a drawer, or what happens when you push an object near the edge of a table. That kind of physical intuition has to be built in from the start, in how you represent the world, how you collect data, and how you design the model to predict consequences of actions rather than just recognize things.

So at some point we asked ourselves: if we were designing this from scratch, starting from what a robot actually needs to do in a real home or a real factory, would we end up with the architecture we have now? And the honest answer was no. That's when we decided it was worth the pain to rebuild rather than keep patching. It was a hard decision because it meant throwing away things that were working okay, but I think "okay" isn't good enough if you want robots that people can actually rely on every day.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics had borrowed models and training methods from language and internet-image work, then explains that physical robots require different capabilities and constraints.

r002.rationale: It says the team chose to rebuild after concluding the existing architecture did not meet real-world needs, but does not say they could not redirect digital-world model developers.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came from a kind of frustration. For a long time we were building what I'd call "video models wearing a robot costume." We'd take an architecture designed to generate beautiful pixels, bolt on some action tokens, and hope that understanding of the physical world would somehow emerge. And in demos it looked great. But the moment you put it on a real arm in a real kitchen, you discover that the model has no idea that a cup has weight, that a door resists you, that if you push a plate too far it falls off the table. It had learned the appearance of physics, not physics itself.

So the question we kept asking was: what does a robot actually need from a model? And the answer is not photorealism. The robot doesn't care whether the reflection on the glass is correct. It cares about things like: if I apply this force here, where will the object be in half a second? Is this surface stable enough to put something on? What's the consequence of my action, not just the next frame? Those are questions about dynamics, contact, causality. And once you write that list down, you realize almost nothing in a conventional generative pipeline is optimized for it. The data is the wrong data, the objective is the wrong objective, the evaluation is the wrong evaluation.

That's why we decided it couldn't be a patch. We had to go back to the foundation and ask what the model should be representing. In our case that meant putting state and interaction at the center, treating the visual signal as evidence about the world rather than as the product, and training on data where the model is forced to predict outcomes of actions, including failures. Failures turned out to be incredibly important, because a model that has only seen successful demonstrations has never learned what "wrong" feels like.

It was painful, I'll admit. We threw away a lot of work that was genuinely impressive by the old standards. But I think that's the honest path. If you want a model that can act in the world, it has to be built around the world, not around the camera.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts models optimized to generate realistic pixels with robots’ need to understand physical dynamics, contact, and action outcomes.

r002.rationale: The response says the existing approach was inadequate and motivated a rebuild, but does not say that an inability to redirect digital-world model developers motivated the decision.

astra-6.text:
Because in robotics, the physical world has to be the starting point. A model can give a convincing answer, but a robot has to take an action—and that action has consequences. It needs to understand what it can reach, how an object might move, and what to do when things don’t go as expected.

That changes how you approach the model. You work backward from what the robot needs to accomplish: what it must perceive, how it should connect perception to action, and how it can learn from feedback. The goal is to build something that can act reliably in the world, where information is incomplete and conditions keep changing.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a model producing a convincing answer with a robot needing to act reliably in the physical world, communicating the mismatch between answer-focused models and robotics needs.

r002.rationale: The response gives physical-world needs as the reason to work backward from robot tasks, but does not mention being unable to redirect digital-world model developers as the motivation.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the starting point was a simple question: what does a robot actually need to do in the physical world? It has to perceive its surroundings, act, and respond when the result is different from what it expected. A model can look very capable in a demonstration, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it can handle that whole loop reliably.

So I wanted to reverse the direction of the work. Instead of starting with a model and asking where we could apply it, we start with the physical task and ask what capabilities the model needs. That changes how you think about the data, the architecture, and especially how you evaluate progress. The goal is to make the robot useful under real conditions, where there’s uncertainty and every action has consequences.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts model capability in demonstrations with reliable physical-world performance, but it does not identify digital-world application objectives as the source of the mismatch.

r002.rationale: The response says the speaker wanted to reverse the direction of the work, but does not say that inability to redirect digital-world model developers motivated the decision.
